lesson.title: Why e^x Is Its Own Derivative
lesson.summary: The natural exponential function e^x is the unique function whose derivative equals itself, a property that falls directly out of the limit definition of the derivative.
lesson.body:
Every exponential function of the form b^x has a derivative that is proportional to itself, but only one base makes that proportionality constant equal to exactly 1. That base is called e, an irrational number approximately equal to 2.71828, and the function e^x is the unique exponential whose tangent line slope at any point matches the height of the graph at that exact point. This is not just a convenient fact to memorize. It is essentially how e gets defined in the first place: mathematicians pick e to be the base for which the exponential curve grows at a rate that matches its current value, with no extra scaling factor needed.

You can verify this using the limit definition of the derivative, the same tool behind every derivative rule you have learned so far. Start with f(x) = e^x and build the difference quotient [e^(x+h) - e^x] / h. Since e^(x+h) equals e^x times e^h by the laws of exponents, factor e^x out of the numerator to get e^x times [(e^h - 1) / h]. The factor e^x does not involve h at all, so it slides straight out of the limit, leaving f'(x) = e^x times the limit as h approaches 0 of (e^h - 1)/h. That remaining limit is exactly the slope of e^x at x = 0, and by the way e is defined, it equals 1. Substituting gives f'(x) = e^x times 1, which is simply f'(x) = e^x.

To put this to work, differentiate g(x) = 4e^x - 7x^2 + 2. Each term differentiates on its own thanks to the sum and constant multiple rules you already know: the derivative of 4e^x is 4e^x, since a constant factor passes straight through the exponential derivative; the derivative of -7x^2 is -14x by the power rule; and the derivative of the constant 2 is 0. So g'(x) = 4e^x - 14x. As a check, notice that at x = 0 the exponential piece 4e^x equals 4, and its derivative there is also 4e^0 = 4, exactly matching the self replicating property that makes e^x special in the first place.

This self derivative property is the reason e^x appears whenever a quantity's rate of change is proportional to how much of it currently exists, such as idealized population growth, continuously compounded interest, or radioactive decay once the sign is reversed. If a quantity y satisfies the equation dy/dx = y, then y must equal C times e^x for some constant C, and no other elementary function reproduces itself under differentiation the way e^x does. That singular property is what makes e the natural base for continuous growth models rather than an arbitrary choice among infinitely many possible exponential bases.

Because the derivative of e^x combines so cleanly with the linearity rules already in your toolkit, it becomes the essential building block for everything that follows in this chapter, from finding the derivative of a^x for other bases to handling exponentials nested inside other functions once the chain rule enters the picture.
